## Description
The PR splits the GUI rendering into two passes, if enabled in the advanced settings. In a first pass, all opaque elements get rendered in front to back order. In the second one, all elements with alpha blending enabled get rendered.

To enable it, you need to supply the following setting(s):
```
<advancedsettings>
  <gui>
    <fronttobackrendering>true</fronttobackrendering>
    <geometryclear>false</geometryclear>
  </gui>
</advancedsettings>
```

It also changes some details with clearing the screen, depending on the "geometryclear" setting. On tiling GPUs, it is better to clear the screen at the beginning of a frame, as it avoids loading previous frame content. But even on modern GPUs, a straight glClear() might be better, as the overdraw by the drawcall can be avoided. Screen clears can be done by copy engines, thus relieving the processing units.

Currently, this only works on GL/GLES. A DX dev would need to step up to bring this feature to Windows. It shouldn't be too hard tho.


## Motivation and context
Overdraw (rendering to a pixel multiple times) is very common with current skins. It is a main factor of framerate drops in Kodi.

By avoiding the rendering of covered areas, the overdraw can be reduced. Depending on the view, I could observe a reduction in overdraw by up to 50%. 

The performance uplift is depending on the GPU. Some desktop GPUs might experience slight performance degradation on very light skins. But on average, it should be a net performance gain. On most ARM GPUs, access to the depth buffer is free. Depending on how the GPU is rejecting covered polygons, it might skip rasterization or the fragment thread creation, saving GPU cycles. In any case, the texture bandwidth needed is most likely reduced, as the occluded areas don't need to be textured.

## How has this been tested?
GL and GLES compile and run fine on X11. On my RX570, I've seen performance improvements of up to 40% with some Estuary views.

## What is the effect on users?
More performance. I've hidden the improvement under an advanced setting, so it should not make a difference per default.

Previous code did not cover "static" vertices when rendering font. 

The whole font geometry handling is not suited for modern GPUs (setting up vertex data EVERY frame). But that's a story for another day.

Works without issue on my AMD Ryzen 7 5700U (Wayland/GL/Mesa 22.3.6). There is no difference in performance because the GUI already renders with 60 fps @ 4K without this change.

I also made tests with compiler sanitizers and Valgrind, both without issues detected.

Edit: One thing I noticed is that the `visualizedirtyregions` option in advancedsettings.xml is broken with this optimization.

Dirty region visualization should work now. 

I've also optimized the rendering order of buttons and bordered elements. It doesn't change the resulting image, but it reduces overdraw if both of the textures used in such elements are opaque.
I've changed how quads are handled. The dimming screensaver was broken before.

comments:
What I think is happening is on a channel change, there is no video texture available for Kodi to present. On GLES, we don't blank the pixels which are usually covered by the video, resulting in undefined values at those positions.

The linked PR fixes the issue by accident, as front to back rendering needs a bit more care when clearing the screen. A full screen triangle is drawn in this case.

Ideally, I think we should keep presenting the last video frame, but having a black screen is better than this behaviour.
Should be fixed in v22 with https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/pull/22919

review_comments: I don't have GL or GLES, but shouldn't m_depth be passed somewhere in there? it doesn't default to -1 in gles_shader.vert, unlike the GL cases that have a different default vertex shader.

See a bit lower in GUIVideoControl::Render, it seems to handle alpha. I don't know skinning and am going to guess but it looks like it could be overlaid on something else (maybe with tweened alpha for example).
That would mean it should have a proper depth and not be systematically at the back. If alpha is 255 then it should probably be part of the front to back pass.

It has to be in the back to be consistent across all platforms. When doing hardware rendering on ARM, the HW compositor draws the video layer below the GUI layer. It can't be somewhere in between GUI elements*.
I'm not sure about the alpha part, but I think that's a relic from the past. We can't have alpha for video layers on some ARM devices.
And it should be the first element in the back to front pass. We know that it is the furthest element to render, so we don't need to update the depth buffer.
*to display the video "between" layers on ARM systems, we could draw an placeholder element where the video "shines through" from below.
